openingWhy: This week our own trailer checks caught a low SABA, an empty one, and an SCBA out of hydro — before one hand staked his lungs on any of them. Ownership isn't a poster on the wall. It's a bottle that's full because somebody checked it.
leadershipThought: Twelve weeks is a starting point. The discipline you've built here is what you take into every job after this. Familiarity is where shortcuts are born. Do job 500 the same way you did job 1.

specialFocus.title: Full Circle — Where Twelve Weeks Took Us
specialFocus.standardLabel: The Twelve — What Each Week Left Behind
specialFocus.why:
Twelve weeks ago, on June 15th, we started this thing with Energy Isolation and a promise that it wouldn't be another safety program that dies in week three. This morning it's finished. So before we launch the next cycle tomorrow, look at what actually happened — not what we hoped, what the numbers say happened.

Form compliance, by month, this year: January 80%. February 76%. March 79%. April 79%. May 80%. Five straight months stuck under 80 — that was us before. Then June, the month this program launched: 88%. July 84. August 84. September so far: 86 and climbing. The needle didn't move because anybody got yelled at. It moved because 5:30 every morning, this crew sat down and talked about the work.

The writing: 764 field write-ups now sit in our lessons library — 195 in June, 169 in July, and here's the one that matters: 360 in August. July dipped. That's the month every program dies, when the newness wears off. Ours came back double. 53 different hands have written into that library. Stop-work authority was used 100 times in the last month alone, and every single one of the 459 forms that answered “did we leave it better than we found it” said yes.

That's where we've come from. Not from unsafe to safe — you were never cowboys. From habits that lived in a few good hands to habits that live in the whole crew. Take two minutes this morning and walk the twelve below — every one of them is now something we do, not something we covered.
standard: Wk 1 — Ownership / Energy Isolation: the job is mine even when the lockout is somebody else's. Verify the isolation, never assume it.
Wk 2 — Communication / Breaking Containment: the first break is a conversation before it's a wrench. Bleed, verify, then open.
Wk 3 — Accountability / Line of Fire: know where the energy goes when it lets loose, and don't stand there. Watch each other's positioning.
Wk 4 — Professionalism / Mobile Equipment: spotters spot, taglines get their own hands, and the swing radius belongs to nobody.
Wk 5 — Coaching Others / Confined Space: a permit isn't rescue capability. A name and a plan is. Teach the new hand why.
Wk 6 — Situational Awareness / Driving: the most dangerous iron we run has a windshield. Fatigue and the phone kill more hands than H2S.
Wk 7 — Problem Solving / Hot Work: decide before the pressure arrives. Know the muster point before the alarm, the fire watch before the spark.
Wk 8 — Building Culture / Bypassing Safety Controls: small deviations don't stay small. Correct them when the cost is low — character is what happens when nobody's watching.
Wk 9 — Precision / Excavation: right thing, right order, before the ground opens. The locate flag tells you where to look; your eyes tell you what's there.
Wk 10 — Planning / Safe Mechanical Lifting: the lift plan is written standing still. Nobody improvises with a suspended load.
Wk 11 — Standards / Working at Height: six feet is measured from where you'd land. Validated rescue means a name, not an assumption.
Wk 12 — Discipline / Work Authorization: if it isn't on a ticket it isn't a Canon job. Do job 500 the way you did job 1.

scenarios.title: Tomorrow, We Go Again
scenarios.body:
Tomorrow morning this board flips to Week 1 of Cycle 2, and we open with Breaking Containment. Somebody's going to think it: “we already did this one.” Here's why that's wrong.

First: the crew that walks in tomorrow is not the crew that heard it in June. We've added hands since then who have never sat through a containment week — the newest guy on your location learned first breaks by watching you, and cycle 2 is where he finds out why you do it that way. Second: you're not the same hands either. In June you listened to scenarios. Since then this crew wrote 764 of its own — real first breaks, real trapped pressure, real calls made at real locations. When we work Breaking Containment this time, the material is yours: Jordan calling out trapped pressure behind a gauge, Ralph holding the hold point while the air cleared on a first break, two crews airing a vessel to zero before anybody cracked a flange. Cycle 1 taught the standard. Cycle 2 holds the standard up against what you actually did — and that's a different meeting.

And third, the honest one: twelve weeks builds a habit, and habits decay without maintenance. That compliance number climbed when we started meeting every morning and it will slide the quarter we decide we've graduated. There is no graduating. That's the whole point of a loop.

questions: Of the twelve, which one actually changed how you work — not which was interesting, which one you now do differently on location?
Which week would you have run differently — wrong scenarios, wrong emphasis, missed what actually matters in the field? Cycle 2 can fix it, but only if you say it now.
The numbers say June jumped to 88% and July dipped before August came back. You lived those months — what actually happened out there?
Who taught you something during this cycle — in a meeting, on a location, in a write-up? Name them out loud.
What does the newest hand on your crew need cycle 2 to give him that cycle 1 gave you?
specialFocus.nonNegotiable: Twelve topics, twelve weeks, one crew. Tomorrow we start the loop again with Breaking Containment — because the standard isn't something we finished, it's something we keep.
